title: The Last Iron Lung Users Are Gone, but Polio Still Isn't
excerpt: With the deaths of Paul Alexander and Martha Lillard, the iron lung era has ended in the United States — yet experts warn that the virus remains a global threat, particularly as vaccine hesitancy grows.
body:
• Paul Alexander, who contracted polio at age six in 1952, spent 72 years in an iron lung and died in March 2024 at 78 — holding the Guinness World Record for longest time in the device.
  • Martha Lillard, the last American to rely on an iron lung, died on June 26, 2026, at 78, marking the end of the iron lung era in the United States.
  • Polio remains endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan, and vaccine-derived poliovirus continues to cause hundreds of paralysis cases worldwide each year.
  • India, declared polio-free in 2014, offers a model for finishing the global eradication effort — but the virus still circulates in neighboring Pakistan.

On a hot summer day in 1952, six-year-old Paul Alexander of Dallas, Texas, developed a headache and a fever. Within days, he could not move, speak or swallow. Doctors diagnosed polio — three years before Jonas Salk's vaccine became widely available.

Almost completely paralyzed from the neck down, Alexander was placed inside an iron lung, a steel cylinder that would become his constant companion for the next seven decades. He died on March 11, 2024, at age 78. Less than two and a half years later, on June 26, 2026, Martha Lillard of Shawnee, Oklahoma — the last known American to depend on an iron lung — also died at 78, from complications of long-haul COVID-19.

Their deaths close a chapter in medical history. But the disease that put them in those machines has not been closed at all.

A Life Lived Beyond the Machine

Alexander refused to let the iron lung define him. He graduated high school with honors, earned a law degree from the University of Texas at Austin in 1984, and practiced law for years — representing clients in court in a three-piece suit and a modified wheelchair.

"I never gave up, and I'm not going to."

— Paul Alexander, in a 2021 interview

"He mastered the technique — called "frog breathing" — and was rewarded with a dog named Ginger."

In 2020, he published a memoir, Three Minutes for a Dog: My Life in an Iron Lung, tapping out every word using a pen attached to a stick held in his mouth. The title referred to a childhood deal with his therapist: breathe independently for three minutes, and get a puppy. He mastered the technique — called "frog breathing" — and was rewarded with a dog named Ginger. Late in life, he amassed more than 330,000 followers on TikTok sharing his story.

The End of an Era

Lillard's story paralleled Alexander's. She contracted polio on her fifth birthday in 1953 and slept in an iron lung every night for 73 years. She attended high school through a phone intercom system, volunteered at an animal shelter, composed music for left-handed piano, and married her longtime partner in February 2026 — just months before her death.

"They told her she wasn't supposed to live past 20 years old," her sister Cindy McVey told the Associated Press.

Iron lungs were a common sight in polio wards during the 1940s and 1950s, when annual outbreaks paralyzed more than 15,000 Americans, mostly children. By 1959, roughly 1,200 people relied on the devices, according to the Smithsonian. By 2004, just 39 remained. With Lillard's death, the count is zero.

The Virus That Hasn't Gone Away

Polio was eliminated from the United States in 1979 and from India in 2014. But the virus remains endemic in Pakistan and Afghanistan, and a mutated form — vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 — continues to cause 300 to 500 cases of paralysis worldwide each year, according to the WHO. In 2022, a man in Rockland County, New York, developed paralytic polio in a community with low vaccination rates — the first U.S. case in nearly a decade.

"People think that polio is gone, but that virus is not gone."

— Paul Offit, director, Vaccine Education Center, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia

India's Victory — and the Unfinished Fight

India's polio eradication stands as one of the great public health achievements of the 21st century. The country reported its last case on January 13, 2011, and was officially certified polio-free by the WHO in 2014 — a remarkable feat in a nation where the disease once paralyzed tens of thousands of children each year. The success relied on a massive network of health workers administering oral vaccines across rural and urban communities.

But wild poliovirus type 1 continues to circulate in neighboring Pakistan, and public health experts warn that even countries with high vaccination rates face risk if coverage slips. In the United States, approximately 93 percent of children are vaccinated against polio by age two, but the number of families claiming nonmedical vaccine exemptions has been rising steadily, reaching a record 3.3 percent of kindergarteners in the 2023–2024 school year.

The iron lung is now a museum piece. The lesson embedded in the lives of Paul Alexander and Martha Lillard — that complacency around vaccination carries real consequences — is not.
image_caption: Paul Alexander in his iron lung in 1986. He contracted polio at age six in 1952 and spent the next 72 years in the device, becoming the Guinness World Record holder for longest time in an iron lung.
nri_angle: India eliminated polio in 2014 through a massive vaccination campaign — a public health triumph the diaspora can take pride in. But with wild poliovirus still circulating in neighboring Pakistan and vaccine hesitancy growing globally, the story remains unfinished.
